newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia's Golkar sweeps to election victory.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia's Golkar sweeps to election victory.

text.p: Indonesia's ruling Golkar swept to a general election win on Friday with a percentage of the vote that even surprised party leaders despite the fact victory was a foregone conclusion.
Golkar, in power for most of President Suharto's 30-year rule, was assured of winning even before the start of a campaign that saw the worst political violence in the country in three decades.
The party had taken a record 74 percent of the 105 million votes counted out of a potential 125 million by Friday evening, up from 68 percent in the last poll in 1992.

"It surprises us because according to our calculations we thought we can reach only 70 or 71 percent," Abdul Gafur, one of the party's seven chairmen, told Reuters. Its previous record was 73.17 percent in 1987.

Of the other two parties permitted to contest Thursday's elections for a national parliament and regional and local assemblies, the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) had 23 percent, up from 17 percent in 1992, while the fragmented Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) plummeted to three from 15 percent.

The PPP and the Independent Election Monitoring Committee (KIPP) both complained of widespread election irregularities. PPP campaign manager Jusuf Sjakir said the party would decided next week whether it accepted the outcome.

Analyst Dewi Fortuna Anwar, of the Centre for Information and Development Studies (CIDES), said she believed the vote itself was probably free, but the system set up by Suharto was stacked against the minority parties.
"In terms of the election itself, I think it's free, so it is not the election itself that is the problem. If Golkar wins, I don't think it will be because of vote manipulation or anything like that.
"It's just that conditions are made which means it is quite hard for Golkar to lose," she said.
Analysts said the Golkar victory in the world's fourth most populous nation would have little effect on government makeup or policy.

The key election will come next March when Suharto, 75, is widely expected to seek a seventh five-year term. The country is keenly interested in who he will select for a running mate, a potential successor given the president's age.

There were no reports of major trouble on Friday, although the death toll in election-related violence during separatist guerrilla attacks in the troubled former Portuguese colony of East Timor rose to 17.

Financial markets were steady and the rupiah strengthened against the dollar. The stock market opened with a spurt, but fell back on reports of rioting on Madura island on Thursday night by a Moslem crowd angered by Golkar's gains in a PPP stronghold.
Economic analysts said investors were keeping a wary eye out for any further violence, particularly in Jakarta by PPP supporters unwilling to accept Golkar's vote.
By Friday evening, Golkar had 57 percent of the vote in the capital of 10 million people, PPP 41 percent and the PDI two percent.

The collapse of the PDI, which had 15 percent in 1992, followed a bitter leadership feud after party chairman Megawati Sukarnoputri -- popular daughter of Indonesia's late founding president Sukarno -- was ousted by a government-backed rival last year.
Megawati had refused to vote and told her supporters to steer clear of the "official" PDI if they went to the polls, but she was unavailable for comment on Friday.

Political analysts said both the PPP and Golkar had reaped a benefit from the PDI split, but there was no immediate indication of the size of Golput (White Party), the Indonesian term for dissidents who spoil their ballots or abstain in protest.
